ai.definition: Carbon-negative mycelium bricks are construction materials created through the growth of mycelium, the vegetative part of fungi, which binds together agricultural waste and other organic matter to form strong, durable blocks.
ai.howItWorks: Mycelium is introduced to a mixture of agricultural waste or other suitable substrates. Over time, the mycelium consumes these materials, growing into a dense network that forms the brick structure. Once matured, the bricks are harvested and dried, ready for use in construction.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the need for sustainable building materials with reduced carbon footprints and waste management solutions.
ai.manufacturing: The manufacturing process involves preparing the substrate mixture, inoculating it with mycelium spores, incubating until fully grown, harvesting, and drying. This method requires controlled environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity.
ai.buildProcess: Mycelium bricks are typically grown in bioreactors or trays filled with the substrate. Once matured, they are removed from their growing medium, dried, and then used directly in construction.
ai.costDrivers: Costs primarily depend on the availability of agricultural waste as a substrate, energy consumption for incubation and drying processes, and initial setup costs for bioreactor infrastructure.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The technology is expected to grow in adoption as more projects are implemented and its benefits become clearer.
ai.regulation: Currently, there are no specific regulations governing mycelium bricks. However, local building codes may need to be updated or clarified for their use.
ai.risks: Potential risks include variability in growth rates due to environmental conditions, contamination of the substrate by pathogens, and challenges in scaling up production while maintaining quality.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable based on market acceptance, competition from traditional building materials, and government incentives or subsidies for sustainable practices.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development could focus on optimizing growth conditions, expanding the range of substrates used, and improving mechanical properties to meet various construction needs.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking.

glossary.def: A controlled environment for growing mycelium, often used in industrial-scale production.
The material that serves as food and support for the growth of mycelium.

subsystems.name: Fungal inoculum
subsystems.role: the living binder that grows through and fuses the substrate.

subsystems.name: Lignocellulosic substrate
subsystems.role: waste biomass that provides nutrients and bulk.
parts: chopped straw, hemp hurds or corn stalks

subsystems.name: Mould and forming
subsystems.role: shapes the mixture into brick geometry.

subsystems.name: Growth chamber
subsystems.role: provides the warm, humid, dark conditions for mycelium to colonise.

subsystems.name: Processing and finishing
subsystems.role: stops growth, hardens the brick and adds surface properties.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the substrate
buildSteps.detail: Agricultural waste is chopped to a consistent size and pasteurised with heat or steam to kill competing microbes.

buildSteps.title: Inoculate
buildSteps.detail: The cooled substrate is mixed with mycelium spawn so the fungus is distributed throughout.

buildSteps.title: Fill moulds
buildSteps.detail: The mixture is packed into brick-shaped moulds, often with a liner to allow easy removal.

buildSteps.title: Incubate
buildSteps.detail: Moulds sit in a warm, humid, dark chamber for one to three weeks while mycelium grows through every particle, binding them together.

buildSteps.title: Demould
buildSteps.detail: Once the brick holds its shape, it is removed from the mould.

buildSteps.title: Stop growth
buildSteps.detail: The brick is heated or dried to kill the mycelium and prevent further growth, which also hardens the composite.

buildSteps.title: Finish
buildSteps.detail: Surfaces can be sanded, pressed for density, or coated to resist moisture and fire.

buildSteps.title: Cure
buildSteps.detail: Finished bricks are conditioned to stabilise moisture content before use.

prerequisites.why: pure cultures are needed to avoid contamination.
a steady supply of cheap, clean biomass is required.
to scale up from lab to factory.
to stop growth without adding much energy.

pathway.milestone: niche products: packaging, acoustic panels and insulation boards
non-load-bearing bricks and blocks for interior walls and temporary structures
hybrid bricks reinforced with natural fibres or bio-resins for load-bearing use
standardised, carbon-negative building materials with certified fire and moisture performance
pathway.unlocks: mainstream construction and carbon storage at scale.
